directions.brief: Subject built on P2 Diagram + trace; drawing language: oscilloscope trace.
Subject built on P3 Trace as subject; drawing language: typeset diagram.
Subject built on P4 Stack in depth; drawing language: orthographic elevation.
Subject built on P5 Field and figure; drawing language: survey plan.
Subject built on P11 Instrument stack; drawing language: patent section. This pattern is outside the category's column: say why this machine is the exception, or say plainly it doesn't fit.

variants.subject: A dual-channel scope: the partial spectrum and its decay slope on the left graticule, the summed output waveform on the right.
controls: settle: rotation; the ch2 decay line (level in dB against time, so an exponential settle is a straight line) swings from steep (0.1 s) to nearly flat (10 s), about 56 degrees.
layers: count; the ch1 spectrum gains lines, one per partial, from 2 to 64 across the log-frequency graticule.
stir: shape; the output trace (one mutable outline, 64 points) gains high-partial ripple and sharpens its edges as stir lifts the upper partials.
grain: position; each spectrum line slides off its harmonic tick by a fixed seeded amount, so coarse grain reads as an inharmonic, scattered comb.
risks: Easy to drift into 'oscilloscope', which says nothing new (P3 pitfall applies to the right half).
Three graticules make it read as a dashboard of meters; the subject is split in three boxes, not one object.
At 64 layers the log-spaced top lines bunch under 3 px; cap or thin the upper octave.
Grain's sideways slide is ~3-6 px per line, below the 24 px position floor; needs more travel or shape help.
Settling itself (the sinking) only shows on notes; at rest the screen is a static spectrum.

variants.subject: The stirred wave printed big as a textbook figure, its component partials drawn small beneath it hanging in a band that sinks toward a stippled silt bed.
controls: settle: position; the band of component curves hangs high under the wave at long settle and drops onto the stipple bed at short settle (about 26 px).
layers: count; one printed component curve per partial is added under the wave (capped at eight visible, labelled k2 to kN).
stir: shape; the main wave (the one bright mutable outline) gains high-partial ripple and steeper edges.
grain: scale; the stipple dots of the bed grow from fine silt (3 px) to coarse sand (6 px).
risks: The component band reads as water hatching at 1:1; spacing is exactly at the 7 px limit and amplitude only 2 px.
Layers has to cap at eight curves, so 16..64 differ only in the label; count floor (12 items) fails above 8.
Grain on the bed is small and low-grey; scale 2x of 3 px dots may still under-read for a score-3 control.
Settle shown as a position is a snapshot of a time; it explains 'how far they've sunk', not the rate.

variants.subject: Octave bands of partials as flat plates in elevation, stepping back from the fundamental on the ground line, the upper plates lifted off their dashed settled positions.
controls: settle: position along the stack; the bright plate (the settle front, the band still falling) moves from the front plate at 0.1 s to the back plate at 10 s.
layers: count; one plate per octave band (k1, k2, k3-4, k5-8 ...), from 2 plates at 2 partials to 7 plates at 64.
stir: position; plates lift vertically off their dashed settled lines, more the further back (higher) they are, up to ~46 px for the top band.
grain: shape; the bright plate's top edge goes from a fine serration to coarse teeth.
risks: Settle and stir both use position, on different parts and axes (bright marker along the stack vs vertical lift); a reviewer may call it a shared channel.
Count by octave grows slowly (2 to 7 plates), under the 12-item floor though it is more than doubling.
Plates read as shelves or a bar chart at 1:1; the elevation conventions (ground hatch, hidden settled lines, dimension ticks) carry the language and must stay crisp.
Grain only shapes one plate; a score-3 control on a 230 px edge with 1.5-5 px teeth is borderline.

variants.subject: A survey plan of a settling basin: a bright silt plume spreading from the inlet over the faint contoured bed, with its deposit lens on the flow line and one chainage station per partial along the foot.
controls: settle: scale; the plume grows from 0.7x to 1.3x along the flow line (slow-settling silt stays suspended and travels further).
layers: count; chainage stations along the bottom strip, one tick per partial, every fourth numbered.
stir: shape; the plume's edges lobe and billow (high partials lifted) from a smooth fan to a churned outline.
grain: position; the deposit lens slides upstream toward the inlet as grain coarsens (coarse grains drop out first), about 100 px.
risks: The strip of stations is close to a 'strip of cells' at rest (craft: picture, not panel); it earns its place only because it is the partial count.
Contours under 1.5 px (hairline field, lint warns) may vanish on the panel; check on device.
The plume is a metaphor for the spectrum, not a plot of it: stir lobing doesn't literally show which partials lifted.
A blob outline can slide toward an organic or icon-like shape (an earlier draft read as a fish); keep it a fan.

variants.subject: A glass settling column cut open like a patent figure, its partial strata stacked from the bed up to a bright interface, a hinged stirring arm and suspended grains above.
controls: settle: position; the bright interface between settled strata and suspension sits low for a fast settle and high for a slow one (about 100 px).
layers: count; one stratum line per partial from the bed up, to the interface (capped near 24 visible).
stir: rotation; the stirring arm swings on its pivot from hanging straight (0) to 40 degrees (100).
grain: scale; the suspended particles grow from 3 px to 6 px.
risks: Stretch: P11 is for instruments people know by sight, and a settling column (Imhoff cone, elutriation tube) isn't one most players know; recognition is not free here, so the pattern's main reason doesn't hold. Honest verdict: it doesn't fit the pattern well; it survives as a section drawing (closer to P1) of the machine's own metaphor.
Layers counted as strata loses legibility past ~24 lines; strata hide above the interface at slow settle.
The arm rotating is a literal stir, but stir in the DSP lifts high partials; the arm angle doesn't show which partials rise.
Hatched walls are many small static paths; fine for budget but check hatch spacing (5 px) on device.
variants.stretch: Doesn't fit P11 honestly: silt has no instrument the player knows by sight. The column is the machine's own metaphor drawn as an instrument; keep it only if the owner wants a literal object.

rejection.reason: None land. Five new, unique variations.
